title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
claim: Independently built agents fail to coordinate in a minimal signaling game, but adding a coordination-friendly definition makes them reliably pick the safe option.
layout: 2 panels: cartoon game scenario left, paired heatmaps right comparing without/with CFD
description: The left panel is a stick-figure cartoon of the Cat & Dog game. Alice stands beside a light switch, with a cat/dog image pair on the ground in front of her. A tall black wall stands between her and Bob, with a lit and an unlit light bulb above it and an up arrow showing the wall can be removed. Bob stands on the right with a thought bubble holding cat and dog pictures and a question mark, meaning he must guess the animal. The right panel shows two 4x4 heatmaps of cross-play scores, Alice (rows) against Bob (columns), for GPT-5.2, Grok 4.1 Fast, Gemini 3 Pro and DeepSeek V3.2. The left heatmap, 'w/o CFD', has varied scores from -4 to 9 and large standard deviations. The right heatmap, 'CFD', is uniformly green at 5.00 with 0.00 deviation. A viridis colorbar labelled Score sits at the far right.
caption: Cat & Dog coordination game. (Left). Alice observes an animal (cat/dog). She can either bail and end the game for a joint reward of 1, remove the wall for a cost of 5, or use the light bulb to signal for free. Bob either observes the state of the light bulb or the animal if the wall is removed. He can guess the animal (+10/-10) or bail for a reward of 0.5. (Right) XP of text agents in the variable \acs{llm} setting with and without \acs{cfd}. Each cell contains the average score of 10 episodes. Adding the \acs{cfd} leads the agents to consistently pick the safe fallback for a guaranteed reward of $+5$.
abstract: We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where independently developed agents must coordinate at test time. While ZSC has been well studied in the RL literature, far less is known about the performance of LLM agents despite their increasing deployment in such settings. Existing work on LLM coordination often relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share in practice. Moreover, evaluations on complex environments (e.g., Hanabi) make it difficult to pinpoint the sources of coordination failure. In contrast, we focus on simple, general-purpose scaffolds in minimal environments designed to isolate specific coordination challenges. Our results show that even in these controlled settings, frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate, largely due to limited understanding of the coordination problem and weak reasoning about their partner's beliefs. While LLMs introduce semantic information as an additional axis for coordination, they nonetheless fail to exploit this structure effectively. Towards this, we propose Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs) as a principled approach for enabling robust coordination among LLM agents. Finally, we show that CFDs can be discovered automatically, removing the need for manual engineering. Code is available at https://github.com/ahayler/zsc-llm-agents.
